title: Tiered latency prioritization ablation journal
content:
Objective:
Run an empirical ablation of a small, pragmatic scheduler variant we prototyped: tiered-latency-prioritization (TLP). Goal is to see whether grouping incoming requests into latency tiers (short/medium/long) with separate dynamic windows improves p99 tail while preserving throughput and per-tenant fairness.

High-level idea (recap):
- Classify requests at enqueue by estimated remaining token length (cheap heuristic: prompt_tokens + model_max_response_estimate) into 3 tiers: P0 (short, <=32 tokens), P1 (medium, 33-128), P2 (long, >128).
- Maintain per-tier continuous-batching windows with independently tuned timeouts and max_slot sizes.
- Allow cross-tier fast-path: if a P0 batch fills to slot capacity before timeout, flush immediately and preempt P1/P2 slots if necessary.
- Soft-demote tenants that repeatedly preempt to avoid starvation: token-credits decay if preempt count high.

Hypotheses:
1) Short-request latency (p50/p95/p99) will improve because P0 batches are isolated from long tails of P2 requests.
2) Overall GPU throughput (tokens/sec) will not materially decrease; some inefficiency from smaller P0 batches may reduce throughput a bit.
3) Multi-tenant fairness: low-volume tenants may see regressions if soft-demotion parameters are too aggressive.

Experiment config (lab harness):
- Workloads: replay of 48h production traces (mixed tenants) + synthetic microbursts.
- Model: llama-3-small-like (attention profile similar to our CLS baseline) on p4d-equivalent nodes.
- Runtime flags: --tiered-heuristic=length-estimate --p0-timeout=3ms --p1-timeout=8ms --p2-timeout=25ms --max-slot-p0=8 --max-slot-p1=16 --max-slot-p2=32 --enable-soft-demotion=true
- Baselines: current adaptive-windowing continuous-batcher (master) + fixed-window batcher (control).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (request end-to-end), tokens/sec, GPU SM utilization, avg batch size per tier, preempt_count per-tenant, memory copy stalls (CPU->GPU), kernel time breakdowns (cuBLAS, attention kernels), KV cache hit ratio. Tracing via microtrace + perf counters + Nsight traces for selected runs.

Profiling & Observations:
1) Kernel hotspots: across experiments we repeatedly hit an aten::copy path that shows up as CPU blocking during enqueue-to-GPU prep. This manifests as a 2-4ms tail on some P0 flushes when the system is thrashing small allocations. Suspicion: frequent small tensors for short requests cause allocator churn and cross-thread mutex contention.
- Quick mitigation: enable per-thread allocator caches (jemalloc tuned) reduced copy stalls by ~30% in a microbench.

2) cuBLAS scheduling interference: mixing small P0 matmuls with large P2 matmuls on the same stream causes cuBLAS to choose different heuristics; when P0 preempts mid-run it forces stream serialization and triggers kernel re-syncs, increasing latency for both P0 and P2.
- Observation: isolating streams per-tier (dedicated CUDA streams per tier) reduced p99 for P0 by ~12% and reduced preemption serialization events by ~70%.

3) Batch size vs timeout tradeoffs (summary):
- P0: small slot (8) + very short timeout (3ms) gave best p50/p95 for short requests; p99 improved modestly but still sensitive to allocator stalls.
- P1: medium slot (16) + 8ms balanced throughput and latency.
- P2: larger slot (32) with long timeout preserved throughput.
Micro-result: end-to-end p99 across all requests improved by 9% vs master under mixed load. But throughput (tokens/sec) dropped ~4% due to more small batches and less kernel fusion opportunities.

4) Fairness regressions: in multi-tenant replay, a low-volume tenant that sent sporadic P2 requests saw increased completion latency when higher-priority tenants filled P0 frequently and preempted resources. Soft-demotion helped but tuning is sensitive: too-aggressive demotion increases tail for preempting tenant; too-lenient allows starvation.

5) KV cache interaction: P2 long requests rely heavily on KV cache prefill; separating tiers caused less effective prefix coalescing for P1/P2 in some windows, reducing effective cache hit ratio by ~3% and causing small increases in P2 kernel time.

Profiling artifacts & traces collected (high-value):
- Nsight timeline of a microburst where P0 floods and preempts P2 (trace id: nsig-20250225-03).
- eBPF trace showing allocator contention (probe id: ebpf-alloc-20250226).
- microtrace sets with batch boundaries annotated for P0/P1/P2 (stored in perf-bucket s3://redwood-internal/traces/tlp/).

Surprising finds / notes to self:
- Preemption overhead dominated by host-side work (copy + launch) rather than waiting in GPU queue. We overestimated GPU queue contention as the main cause.
- Small-batch penalty stems in part from Python-level serialization in enqueue path; moving critical enqueue hot-path to C++ reduced enqueue CPU time by ~40% and improved P0 p99 by ~6%.
- Demotion parameters interact with admission-control crediting in unexpected ways; need a small simulator to sanity-check parameter sweeps.

Quick config table (text):
- Candidate A (current): adaptive-window master (baseline)
- Candidate B (TLP default): p0=3ms/slot8, p1=8ms/slot16, p2=25ms/slot32, streams-per-tier=3, soft-demote decay=30s
- Candidate C (TLP tuned): p0=2ms/slot6, p1=10ms/slot18, p2=22ms/slot28, streams-per-tier=4, soft-demote decay=15s

Preliminary numeric summary (median of 5 runs on replay):
- Baseline: p99=320ms, p95=48ms, tokens/sec=1.0x
- Candidate B: p99=292ms (-8.8%), p95=44ms (-8.3%), tokens/sec=0.97x
- Candidate C: p99=281ms (-12.2%), p95=42ms (-12.5%), tokens/sec=0.95x (bigger throughput hit but best tail)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is the throughput regression acceptable for hosted API customers at current price points? Run cost-model: expected token-cost delta vs SLA improvement.
- How to formalize preemption budget per-tenant so we can reason about long-term fairness? (Need small simulator).
- Should we prefer stream isolation (extra CUDA streams) or rely on kernel batching heuristics? Memory pressure on some instance types may make extra streams worse. Test on a smaller GPU class.
- Does C++ enqueue path refactor create any compatibility issues with existing Python-only extensions? Need integration test.

Action items (next 2 sprints):
- Build a lightweight simulator for demotion + preemption budget sweeps (owner: Marco).
- Implement per-thread allocator cache in staging and run nightly microburst traces (owner: Sofia).
- Land enqueue-hotpath C++ refactor PR + perf tests (owner: Liam).
- Evaluate cost model for Candidate C vs baseline and present to product next week (owner: Aisha).

Notes for write-up / possible doc candidates:
- This should live as a working journal (this doc) + a short public-facing postmortem if we decide to flip TLP on in prod.
- Keep traces and nsight exports in perf-bucket and link to INF ticket.

Rough TODOs (quick):
- [ ] Add simulator design sketch to this doc (follow-up)
- [ ] Run Candidate C for 24h production replay and check degradation on low-volume tenants
- [ ] Re-run Nsight traces with stream-isolation toggled off/on to measure GPU scheduling effects precisely
- [ ] Draft a short explainer for product on tradeoffs (p50/p95/p99 vs cost)

End-of-journal entry.

-- Aisha
